en: *Commentary on the Meaning of the Ten Stages*, Scroll One.
Because it is adorned, it is metaphorically associated with the celestial abodes (*devasthāna*). To obstruct [the mundane]...
because there is coming and going, and by means of leading conditions one enters into reality, it is metaphorically associated with dwelling in... [the stages].
It abides awaiting an undefiled object.

In the "Chapter on the True Nature and True Character" (*Tattvasvabhāvalakṣaṇa-parivarta*), at this point... [text missing] ...one should understand that the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) is manifested;
it is known by taking the Dharma as its essence.
There were also those whose bodies were [radiant], together with great bodhisattvas.
This clarifies the sixth phrase of the *samyaksambuddha-śraddhā-varga* (the sequence for authenticating the hearing), which concerns the assembly of those who heard the teaching.
Within this section, there are two parts.
First, there is a brief praise of its meaning;
second, from "From these bodhisattvas... onwards, there is an extensive praise of its meaning.
Now, the explanation of this extensive and brief [treatment] is threefold.
First, the broadness and brevity of the teaching;
second, the broadness and brevity of the practice of skillful means;
third, the broadness and brevity of the essential nature.
Regarding the extensive and concise teachings:
the preceding two lines and one commentary are called "concise" because they briefly present the fundamental tenets and briefly praise their significance;
from this point onward, the extensive praise of their significance is termed "extensive."
Regarding the "practice of skillful means":
counteracting [defilements] and manifesting the essence is termed "briefly stated virtues.
As for the "extensively explained body" (vistara-kāya): [text missing].
Although skillful means correspond to the essence, this refers to the true practice of the self-nature within the context of remedial measures; this is termed "concise.
That which constitutes external obstacles to that very essence is termed "extensive."
Regarding the brief lamentation mentioned previously, there are four phrases therein.
[The first] concerns the assembly of great bodhisattvas being equal in number to those gathered here.
The second concerns those who are non-retrogressive.
This first phrase clarifies the firmness of practice.
Regarding the third [phrase],
this one phrase clarifies the application of effort in practice.
Fourth, those who have come from other worlds;
this refers to the place from which they have come.
Now, as for the word "gives":
Regarding "one Buddha gives" and "two Ānandas give":
we shall now explain this according to the Buddha's interpretation.
Since Ānanda was held within [the Buddha's] embrace, one cannot say that he "gave."
Regarding the interpretation according to the principle-teaching (*li-jiao*), it is said that the Great Being (Mahāsattva) receives [the teaching] like a shadow or an echo.
Regarding the interpretation according to the practice-teaching (*xing-jiao*), "receiving" (*yu*) refers to the name of the Buddha’s own essence as the cause.

Regarding the interpretation according to the practice-teaching, Ānanda receives it because he attains the wisdom of hearing and retention (*śrutadhāraṇī-jñāna*), which encompasses his own essence and skillful means (*upāya-caryā*); therefore, it is said that he receives it.
There are three kinds of assemblies of great bodhisattvas:
first, the assembly of reflections and echoes;
second, the assembly of those who are the objects of the teaching.
Third, regarding the number of the assembly:
we now inquire as to how many members constitute the assembly to whom the teaching is addressed, for there are differences among such assemblies.
Herein lies the distinction: there are those who possess limited understanding and can be instructed through dual consultation and exhortation.
Because the distinctions established in the questions and answers concern the teaching, it says "those to whom the teaching is addressed.
Regarding how many such persons there are, although there may be many, because they lack the capacity for understanding and arousal [of the path], it says "how many.
If one considers their stage, those to whom the teaching is addressed are at the final moment of the *mārgajñatā* (path-knowledge) preparatory stage (*prayoga-mārga*).
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, because the true, untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas manifest as reflections within the source of the mind, one may indeed initiate inquiry and realization;
thus, by means of questions and answers, the principle is elucidated externally.
However, during the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and ten practices (*caryā*), one has not yet attained the characteristics of true untaintedness.
Because it may be consulted for clarification, one should consider how many [stages] there are. Following this sequence,

if one speaks of those who are the recipients of the teaching on the *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths), how many are there among the ten practices (*daśaprayoga*) and how many are there among the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*)?
This can be understood by analogy, so there is no need for further elaboration.
However, regarding the two assemblies—the shadows and the echoes—to which these bodhisattvas frequently respond: are they new assemblies or established assemblies?
Another interpretation states that both the new and the old exist; however,
it is only those who possess intermittent roots of goodness [who can attain this].
Regarding the passage on "seeing the Buddha-way and arising at the tree" which spans the six heavens:

if one bases this on the fact that the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) do not cease, it is known that the non-arising [of afflictions] under the tree extends throughout all six heavens; the same applies to the Bodhisattva.
The body manifests in eight locations.
However, as shadows and echoes assist in propagating the Buddha-dharma, whether manifesting or not manifesting, everything is manifested. How many dharmas should one receive?
If they are seen sequentially, it is the characteristic of gradual teaching; if they are seen all at once, it is the characteristic of sudden teaching.
If categorized according to the practice and teaching, there are two:
first, the assembly of the single self-nature;
second, the assembly of expedient practices.
The assembly at the site of enlightenment is fully endowed with the dharma-illumination of the dharma-realm, without deficiency.
From the essence arises cultivation, which relies upon skillful means; these skillful means depend upon conditions.
Because their causal characteristics are distinct and they cannot travel together,
it is said that they come from other directions.
If one relies on the self-substance to practice the dharma-gate of the dharma-realm assembly, how could there be any place where realization and essence are not equal?
"Great" means transcending the Three Vehicles;
it is called "great" because it surpasses even the Shared Teaching and reaches the level of the Shared School's antidotes.

A Bodhisattva—translated in the Qin language as "a sentient being with the mind of the Way"—is so called because such a person inquires into the meaning of the Way; thus, they are termed a "mind of the Way.

Furthermore, there are those of the Great Vehicle and the Two Vehicles who, being unable to practice both tranquility and function simultaneously regarding birth-and-death and nirvana, are designated as "small bodhisattvas."
A Great Being who practices both tranquility and activity, benefiting both self and others with perfect, unobstructed penetration, is called a sentient being of the Great Bodhicitta.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who are nominally designated.
Second is the meaning of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*).
Although a bodhisattva by way of provisional designation possesses understanding and practice, they are unable to achieve perfect penetration because they grasp at names and characteristics.
A bodhisattva of ultimate reality, however, realizes the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as perfectly penetrating and unobstructed; therefore, they are called "Great."
If one were to say that the practice based on the teachings of the *āgama* prior to the [first] bhūmi— like observing an image in a mirror—
is called the "body of skillful means," whereas the true body, which is free from delusion and realizes the nature of the true *dharmadhātu*, is called the "true body."
Because both the provisional and the real assemblies have gathered, it is said that he is "together with a great assembly. There are two kinds of those who are all non-retrogressive:
first, those who are entirely non-retrogressive.

Second, among all things, he clearly understands that all are not grasped, that there is nothing to be grasped, that there is no non-retrogression regarding the portion of others, and no shifting from one’s own portion.
Having thus fulfilled these, he gives rise to superior progress.
While one might wish to enter another stage by giving rise to other states of mind,
this passage clarifies that when a bodhisattva gives rise to superior progress,
they are able to enter another stage; this is called "not turning back from one's own stage" and "not [remaining fixed in] another stage."
One who does not regress does not turn back from their own stage to a lower one;
having already perfected their own stage, they are able to enter superior progress.
Thus, there are broadly and extensively many kinds of non-regression.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
"Non-retrogression" refers to the initial entry into the Dharma-realm; "penetrating to the ultimate source" means being firm and indestructible;

"removing obstacles" means that the seeds of all Buddha-dharmas reside within one's person, with merit and wisdom fully perfected. Regarding the three interpretations, "the worldly path is fulfilled and the supramundane path is established" means that understanding and practice are fused into a single unity.
He is named Vajradhvaja; those who have retreated from the stages eliminate deluded thoughts upon reaching the first bhūmi, realizing the Dharma-realm.
Being born into the family of the Buddhas, their lineage is noble and beyond reproach.

Regarding the statement that the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are not [interrupted] and do not regress: from the eighth stage upward, one enters the flow of the Dharma and moment by moment proceeds toward the ocean of *sarvajñatā*.

In the tenth stage, amidst the clouds of the radiance of all Buddha-dharmas, one rains down the teaching of the Dharma; therefore, this is called "the non-regression of ultimate fulfillment within learning."
There are four kinds of arising:
first, arising through antidotes;
second, arising through practice.
Third, those born from birth;
fourth, those who should be born through transformation.
Regarding "those born from antidotes":
First, birth as a numerical portion;
second, birth through transformation;
third, birth in which self-nature is not established as real.

What is now called "one birth" refers to the fact that the *paricchinna* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) births have already been eliminated, and only the self-nature—which is not truly established—remains as a single birth.
One who practices this "one birth" is one who is truly born.
What is now called "one" refers to the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) that proceeds through the bliss of samādhi.
Second is the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of phenomena;
third is the mind-made body that abides in the same category through non-exertion.
What is here called "one birth" refers to one birth within the stage of non-exertion.
Regarding the eleventh stage, even if one were to undergo a single birth as a vajra-like being,
those who manifest a single birth do so because Bodhisattvas,
through their profound skillful means, take birth in order to discipline and transform sentient beings.
He was born in Tuṣita Heaven;
had he descended to be born among humans, he would have immediately attained Buddhahood.
Because he has only one more birth remaining in Tuṣita, it is said that he will attain bodhi in one lifetime.
Bodhi is termed the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Way (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
It is called "unsurpassed" because it transcends the common teachings of the Three Vehicles.
It is "right" because its principle is absolute and unerring, and thus it is right.
"True" (zhen) means that it is free from the defilements of false imagination and ignorance; thus it is called "true.
"Way" (dao) means that its own essence is perfectly pervasive and unobstructed; thus it is the Way.
As for "coming from another direction": [it refers to those who have come from elsewhere].
Arising from the essence as function,
it is for the sake of gathering function from other realms;
arising from the essence, it is also "other."
"Buddha" refers to the sovereign activity of wisdom and perfect enlightenment within the world.
"World" refers to the sovereign activity within the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
"Both" refers to the convergence of these three types of conditions.
"Coming" manifests that there is no practice that is not gathered;
this refers to the world of sentient beings.
"Gathering" means that the three types are perfectly complete.
"Meeting" (hui) means being perfectly identical with the single flavor;
it may also mean the gathering of practices.
"Meeting" (hui) also signifies the fusion of stages.
This constitutes the second section, which extensively extols the virtues of these bodhisattvas;
it contains four parts.
The first clarifies the virtuous conduct of the bodhisattvas.
The second [section] lists the names of those whose virtues are described below;
the third lists the number of those enumerated below as "such as these.
The phrase "with Vajragarbha as the leader" clarifies who the leaders are.
Within the first section, there are four types of firmness.
The first clarifies the firmness of the stage;
the second, beginning with "being well able to teach and transform," clarifies the firmness of practice.
The third section, beginning with "constantly able to cultivate and accumulate," clarifies the firmness of action (*karma*).
The fourth section, beginning with "thus, these bodhisattvas," clarifies the firmness of extensiveness.
First, regarding the clarification of the firmness of the stages (*bhūmi*):
A state is not established in vain; it takes action as its essence. Action does not operate in isolation, but proceeds by relying upon a state.
Next, the actions are analyzed. Action has no separate creation; it takes the correct activities of body, speech, and mind as its essence. Therefore, next, the karmas are analyzed.
However, as the practice and virtue are vast and all-pervasive, exhausting the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), next is the explanation of the extensive and firm [stages].
Within this section on the stages (*avasthā*), there are two parts. First, the characteristics of the practice within the stage of one's own level (*svabhūmi*).
The section beginning with "Second, the realm of all Tathāgatas" clarifies the characteristics of the practices belonging to the stage of others.
"The various bodhisattvas" refers to bodhisattvas of the preceding life.
"All bodhisattvas" first reveals the causal practices of their own essential nature from the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
Regarding the sphere of wisdom (*jñāna*): its essence manifests externally as luminous and perfectly illuminates the *dharmadhātu*; therefore, it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
Its essence illuminates internally with equality and a single flavor; therefore, it is termed "insight" (*prajñā*).
"Sphere" (*viṣaya*) has the meaning of a delimited boundary;
it may also refer to the boundary of one's practice.
"Mastery" (*vaśitā*) refers to the unimpeded conduct that is pure and mature, having exhausted all obstacles and severed all fetters.
"The realm of all Tathāgatas" means that it is perfectly accomplished as the domain of others.
"All have attained entry" means...
The "superior portion" refers to practice associated with the realization of the profound and substantial essence.
This clarifies the diligent application of understanding and entry.
"Unceasing" refers to the intensely burning practice of listening without interruption.
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"To fully know all the ritual methods of all bodhisattvas is one's own practice;
thus, it is easy to enter the secret treasury of all Buddhas."
This is the practice of others' lands.
"All rely upon wisdom" means that wisdom is the source of the myriad practices.
Regarding the section on the firmness of practice, there are two parts.
The first clarifies the characteristics of one's own practice;
the second, from "In a single moment" onwards, clarifies the characteristics of the practice for others.
Within this section on oneself, there are two parts.
The first clarifies the characteristics of the initial practice;
the second, beginning from "the supernormal power of the wish-fulfilling mind," clarifies the characteristics of the final matured practice.
Regarding the initial cultivation, there are six statements.
The first three clarify the practice of benefiting others;
the subsequent three clarify the practice of benefiting oneself.
However, regarding the practice of a bodhisattva,
there are cases where one first benefits oneself and subsequently benefits others, as it has been said:
"It is impossible for a person who does not practice virtue themselves to teach others to practice virtue."
It is possible that one must first practice virtue oneself before preaching the Dharma to others;
this refers to a bodhisattva who has newly begun their practice and has not yet established the requirement that they must first cultivate it themselves.
Alternatively, there are those who first practice for the benefit of others and subsequently seek their own benefit, as it is said:
"If sentient beings do not attain Buddhahood, I shall never take up perfect enlightenment.
This refers to those who have already established themselves in the bodhisattva practices and whose cultivation has reached full maturity.
Alternatively, one may first enter by way of wisdom (*prajñā*), severing the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) on the path and encompassing practices corresponding to one's own virtues;
thus, self-benefit is placed first.
Subsequently, one enters by way of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), severing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) on the path and encompassing the entry into reality through conditions.
"Being well able to teach and transform others" clarifies the activity of speech (*vākkarman*).
"Universally manifesting at all times" clarifies the activity of body (*kāyakarman*).
"Within a single kṣaṇa" clarifies the activity of mind (*manaskarman*).
This clarifies the benefits of the practice of the three wheels:
it enables sentient beings to sever deluded thoughts and exhaust the obstacles of birth and death;
and through the karma of speech, it enables sentient beings to attain definitive understanding.
Physical action enables sentient beings to attain definitive faith;
mental action causes sentient beings to achieve superior progress.
What is now called "wholesome" is the ultimate state of conformity with the essence [of reality].
The quality of being unobstructed is called "the capacity for teaching and transforming.

Regarding "all worlds," there are three types of causal aggregation (*pratyaya-samudaya*) existing as characteristics: the causal aggregation of conditioned activity, the causal aggregation of unconditioned activity, and the causal aggregation of intrinsic nature.
All these are based on skillful means for entering into practice and are called "the worldly.
"Universally manifesting according to the occasion" clarifies the activity of the body (kāyakarman).
It is said to be "timely" because it benefits beings according to their circumstances.
Furthermore, the true nature of the Dharmakāya constantly provides benefit to sentient beings by acting as both conscious awareness and non-conscious awareness.
As for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there is no place where the body does not manifest.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"If there are sentient beings who should see me as a śrāvaka, I immediately manifest as a śrāvaka; even unto those for whom I am a Mahāyāna practitioner, I manifest as Mahāyāna."
This clarifies that there is no Mahāyāna practice corresponding to the non-contingent, non-objectifying aspect.
Furthermore, "supernatural powers" (abhijñā) refers to swift and unimpeded practice;
"equal matters" (samatā-vastu) refers to the fact that the principle of dependent origination is harmonious and not singular.
Because the dharma-realm is characterized by unimpeded action, it is called "phenomena" (*vastu*).
Regarding "within a single *kṣaṇa*," this clarifies the mental karma (*manas-karman*).
A *kṣaṇa* refers to the interval between every thought-moment, wherein all afflictions are severed and all practices are perfected.

Furthermore, because one can also directly realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and, part by part, truly accord with the path of dependent origination, it is said that "accomplishment" is achieved.
"Fully possessing and not abandoning all bodhisattvas" clarifies the practice for one's own benefit.
Presently, that which is complete is bodhi.
It is the essence of all practices.
One who attains this essence has perfected all practices; because these endure until the end of the future, it is called "complete."
Regarding "not abandoning," the Sūtra therefore says:
"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva guards one dharma, which is the bodhicitta.
As for "that which arises," the bodhisattva-mind takes the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as its principle; because principle and phenomena are fused, it is called "arising."
Therefore, the scripture designates the title of this chapter as "The Chapter on the Arising of the Tathāgata-nature, the Jewel King.

This is not like the emptiness of identical characteristics or the single characteristic of non-substantiality, which maintains a state of uniform quiescence and does not function as dependent origination.
The "Great Vow" refers to the manifestation of the essence of true consciousness; because it aspires toward the ultimate future, it is called a "vow.
"In all worlds" means in every successive world.
"All kalpas" refers to the divisions of time.
“Land” (kṣetra) refers to a location.
“Constantly practicing” means that the bodhisattva constantly practices all bodhisattva deeds throughout the world, the kalpas, and the lands.
Because there is no dharma that does not accord with the teachings when one relies on these practices, it is called “world” (loka).
This is precisely what is explained in detail in the "Chapter on Life Span" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*).
Regarding "kalpas," there is no time that they do not encompass, as stated in the "Chapter on Incalculable Numbers" (*Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*).
Regarding "buddha-fields," there is no place that is not excellent.
Just as a bodhisattva practitioner constantly practices sudden cultivation and fully accumulates what has not been heard,
one who is endowed with merit and wisdom—

though the practices of a bodhisattva are immeasurable— does not transcend the flourishing of merit and wisdom; for they are fully equipped with all virtues and accord with the arising of the path to *sarvajñatā* (omniscience).
"Merit" refers to virtue, while "fortune" refers to wisdom.
As for "the divine power of moving at will," this second section clarifies the characteristics of the final stage of maturation.
Within this, there are also two sets of three phrases.
The first set of three phrases clarifies the mode of practice for the benefit of others;
the latter set of three phrases clarifies the practice for one's own benefit.
The preceding section clarified that the initial cultivation of altruism is also a manifestation of the Bodhisattva’s power and function;
this section clarifies the bestowing of that power. To analyze it further:
When one first cultivates the middle karmic action of the body and accords with this clarity, its practical application is inexhaustible.
When one previously accords with the karmic action of speech and accords with this clarity, that understanding penetrates thoroughly;
being able to exhaust all marks, one attains Great Nirvāṇa.

The preceding mental karma constitutes eight factors of the path of superior progress; this clarifies that the process of dependent origination has been accomplished and one is able to enter the future limit (*aparānta*).
Now, regarding the phrase "in this way," there are three types of intention (*cetanā*).
First, it can reach the ten directions in a single, swift moment of thought.
Second, it reaches everywhere according to its intentional object, pervading all without exception.
Third, it takes all phenomena as its unimpeded object, remaining free from any obstruction.
How much more so for the bodily karma of the Dharma-body, which is likewise inexhaustible?
Since all are accomplished through the dependent origination of true nature as the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-body, how could there be any exhaustion?
This clarifies the mode of the physical karma of matured altruistic conduct.
Those who can reach the wisdom of a bodhisattva are profoundly in accord with true nature and are able to exhaust the limits of the future.
This clarifies the entry through understanding.
As for "expedient means" (upāya), it refers to not abandoning worldly activity while remaining skillful; thus, it is called expedient means.
This clarifies the application of practice within dependent origination.
That "breaking" refers to the completion of practice and the perfection of virtue;
this clarifies that practice has reached its culmination, such that the mental karma is pure and matured, manifesting the characteristics of conduct for the benefit of others.
It is that which enables sentient beings to turn their backs on the worldly path and head toward Nirvana.
It is said they "turn their backs on the world" because they sever the three kinds of false conceptualization.
It is said they "cultivate perfect quiescence" and "realize the harmonious integration with the Dharma-nature."
Because one correctly proceeds toward great tranquility, it is said that one "proceeds toward nirvāṇa.
This aspect of verbal karma is the matured practice of benefiting others.

From the passage beginning "The bodhisattva does not sever... onwards, it clarifies the aspect of matured practice for one's own benefit, wherein both worldly activity and nirvāṇa arise together without obstruction.
This clarifies that through the maturation of practices for one's own benefit, the manifestation of the path of non-abiding is perfected.
"Skillfully roaming" indicates that one has fully attained the resources for practice by realizing the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); thus, it is called "skillfully roaming."
Dhyāna refers to the four dhyānas;
samādhi refers to the four formless concentrations;
and liberation refers to the eight liberations.
Samādhi refers to the three samādhis;
supernormal powers refer to the six abhijñās;
and clarity refers to the three vidyās.
First is the clear knowledge of past lives;
second is the clear knowledge of the divine eye;
third is the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
This is as explained in another chapter.
Alternatively, the first is ignorance, namely the eleven kinds of emptiness;
the second is the bodhisattva’s illumination, namely the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Prajñāpāramitā is called the root of non-negligence.
Third, the "clarity" of all Buddhas refers to the Buddha-eye.
"All that which exists" means it arises perfectly and universally.
"Bestowing and acting" refers to the function of virtue.
"Being well able to manifest" means that the substance accords with the characteristics, such that there is nothing that is not variegated.
This clarifies the completion of the practices that assist the Path.
The realization of the Way through parinirvāṇa is without an agent;
because it is fundamentally not of the present, it is called "without action.
"Sovereignty" refers to the practice of wondrous stillness and non-obstruction.
This concludes the first section concerning the initial cultivation and maturation of self-benefit and benefit for others.
Now begins the second major section, which clarifies the characteristics of the superior progress of the other-portion within a single moment of thought.
The "other-part" (parabhāga) refers to the practices of all Buddhas;
for when one cultivates them, they become one's own part (svabhāga).
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
In the past, I saw that the bodies of the various Buddhas were exceptionally large;
now I see them all as bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
These are the two kinds of manifestations.
To clarify that the practices of a bodhisattva and the practices of a Buddha are non-dual and without distinction,
with the sole difference being whether they are fulfilled or unfulfilled,
there are three points herein.
The first section clarifies physical action (*kāyakarman*); the second section, beginning with "Exhorting and inspiring," clarifies verbal action (*vākkarman*);
and the third section, beginning with "Always with a great mind," clarifies mental action (*manaskarman*).

Furthermore, the first part clarifies the practice of gathering the Dharma (*saṃgraha-dharmapratipatti*), while the second part, beginning with "exhorting and inspiring," clarifies the practice of protecting the Dharma (*dharmarakṣā-pratipatti*).
These two are accomplished within the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
The third section, beginning with "Always with a great mind," clarifies the practice of proceeding toward the path of supreme advancement.
Regarding the phrase "able to reach the ten directions in a single thought-moment":
this means that while the *dharmakāya* is immovable, there is nowhere it does not manifest.
Yet there is no place to which this Dharma does not reach.

Being without "this" or "that," it can manifest in all directions; in reality, there is no coming or going, yet because its forms are nowhere unmanifested, it is said to be able to reach the ten directions.
The exhortation, inquiry, and request refer to the recipient who maintains [the teaching];
it signifies that the correct application of remedies corresponds to the authoritative expression of the doctrine.
As for "maintaining" (*dhāraṇī*), it refers to the excellence of practice being firmly established within oneself and remaining immutable; hence, it is called "maintaining."
The Wheel of Dharma is the true exposition of the ultimate reality that reveals the causes and conditions of phenomena.
It is that which is constantly [turned] by those with the Great Mind.
The internal reality and manifest function pervade the entire dharma-realm.
As for making offerings to the Buddha,
it is the secret dependent origination, wondrously quiescent liberation, which fills the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Because it is non-dual with and corresponds to the path of Perfect Enlightenment, it is called "making offerings to the Buddha.
This clarifies the two forms of wisdom: that of reflection and that of cultivation.
One who can constantly practice them in this way—
Third, clarifying the firmness of one's karma.
Within this, there are three parts.
First, the general training in the three types of action.
The second section, from "From his body he universally manifested... onwards, provides a detailed explanation of the three types of action (*karma*).
The third section, from "All bodhisattvas... onwards, summarizes the three types of action.
As for the actions performed:
To fully assemble and clarify is the first [principle].
As for its body manifesting universally:
its substance is not without variegated patterns.
Regarding those in the borderlands and remote regions,
there is no teaching that does not reach them.
As for those who clearly perceive the three periods of time:
Its essential nature is true luminosity, such that there is nothing it does not illuminate.
As for "fully cultivating and accumulating," it means there are no practices not accumulated and no virtues not realized.
Regarding these merits of the bodhisattvas:
the fourth [verse] clarifies their vastness and firmness;
"immeasurable" refers to reaching the ultimate limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
"Boundless" means it pervades the entire dharma-realm extensively.
Regarding the statement that "it could not be fully expounded even in incalculable eons":
because the practices and virtues of a bodhisattva are so vast that they cannot be described through mere testimony, they cannot be exhausted by speech.
Their names are as follows: next, we shall explain the second section.
Regarding the names of those endowed with virtue (*guṇa*), there are three types of interpretations.

First, according to the *vyāvahārika-śāsana* (teachings for worldly transformation), they are designated in accordance with what sentient beings find appropriate to hear, whether it be concordant or discordant.
As it is said regarding right speech, one establishes the meaning according to the words; yet,
just as the perception of severing fetters does not actually sever the fetters,
it is by means of wisdom that they are severed.
As the Buddha taught that merely contemplating the visualization can eliminate desire,
this is a figurative expression applied to the ultimate meaning,
just as wisdom cuts through the afflictions.
This is the speech of ultimate truth.
This Bodhisattva is named "Thus" (Tathā), such as Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;
his virtuous title is manifested in accordance with sentient beings.
Furthermore, the actual virtues of a bodhisattva do not necessarily have to be placed within these explicit words;
nevertheless, the actual virtues of a bodhisattva are precisely what is expressed by these explicit words.
These two types of speech—whether based on principle and scripture or based on meaning—are both [instances of] speech according to the meaning.

This is because knowing the flavor [of the teaching], knowing the meaning of the clothing, relying on phenomena to manifest the meaning, and understanding the reality through its characteristics serve to reveal the true virtues of the Bodhisattva.
Thirdly, if one relies on the intent of the practice and the teaching, it is intended to clarify the person and demonstrate them.
One who hears the Dharma understands the Dharma and likewise knows the intentions of people, clearly explaining and revealing the Dharma;
one who hears about people understands those people and likewise knows the Dharma, just as the name Vimalakīrti means "Stainless Renown."
One immediately knows the inconceivable and unimpeded dharma-gate of liberation.
Upon merely hearing of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, one immediately knows the dharma-gate of the practices of the Dharma-realm.
Mañjuśrī, the goddess, and the others are all dharma-gates of wondrous wisdom practices.
Vajragarbha and the others also wish to clarify the conduct of bodhisattvas,
which is as vast as the dharma-realm and ultimately coextensive with space.
It is equal and non-dual;
it is the dharma-gate that reveals the true, perfect, and profound essence of one's own being.
Therefore, although the names of the bodhisattvas such as Vajragarbha and others differ, [they are one].
The commentary states:
Generally speaking, there are five types [of naming].
The first is naming based on causes and conditions (*nidāna*).
As for the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, he was named the Bodhisattva "Ever-Crying" (Sadāprarudita) because when he was originally a small child, his parents always called him "Sadāprarudita."
Now, because he constantly pities and grieves for sentient beings, he is called the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita.
Second, his original practice of the Dharma-gate was like that of the Bodhisattva Maitreya;
in the past, when he was a king, [he practiced thus].
Upon arriving at the monastery, he saw that all the bhikṣus sitting in meditation were emitting light,
yet one bhikṣu’s radiance was uniquely superior.
He immediately asked that bhikṣu, "What samādhi are you practicing, such that your radiance is so exceptionally sublime as to surpass those of the other bhikṣus?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"I cultivate the treasury of the samādhi of loving-kindness;
it is the root of all virtues."
Because of this excellence, the King immediately made a vow, saying: "May I, in future ages, constantly cultivate the samādhi of loving-kindness and attain Buddhahood today;
therefore, I shall be named Maitreya."
It was also like when the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was formerly the daughter of a king;
while atop a high tower, she saw a bhikṣu entering an alleyway to beg for oil.
She immediately asked the bhikṣu, "What will you do with the oil you beg for?"
The bhikṣu said,
"Because of my making offerings to the Buddha, I have immediately made a vow:
'May I always offer lamps and light to the Buddha in the future.'"
Today he attained Buddhahood and was named Dīpaṃkara;
according to his original cause, he is called "Lamp-Lighter.
Third, there are differences in the self-benefiting cultivation and entry into the remedies.
Fourth is the distinction of benefiting through the gathering of virtues according to the conditions of transformation,
just as a versatile craftsman is given a name based on his specific function.
Fifth is the distinction of the different causal practices, wherein all dharmas of the self-substance are realized within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
His virtue exhausts the depths of the ocean; he is named Bodhisattva Vajragarbha.
His benefit and profit are inexhaustible; he is called Ratnagarbha, for his utility is like that of jewels.
His own essence, through causal practice, enters the Dharma-realm; he is like Padmagarbha.

To cultivate through conceptualization while clearly understanding its abandonment and detachment is not called the supreme; rather, entering nirvana without severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) is the nature [of this state].
Because it is free from the adornments of conditions, it is named the "Supreme Treasury."
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"For example, one is truly brave only upon ascending to victory;
likewise, a bodhisattva is so called only when they simultaneously eliminate all birth, old age, sickness, and death."
This is what is called the "clarity" of this bodhisattva.
Because this bodhisattva attains non-obstruction regarding all afflictions and their opposing conditions, it is called "supreme.
It is called a "treasury" because the practice of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) can eliminate the darkness of birth and death; therefore, it is called a treasury.

The "Perfect Treasury" (Yuanzang) refers to the conditioned arising of conditions that does not abandon worldly activity; because it is the illumination within darkness, it is called the Perfect Treasury.

The "Pure Perfect Treasury" (Jing Yuanzang) refers to the fact that its own essence is the world itself, which is eternally pure and luminous even amidst darkness, excelling within that purity; therefore, it is called the Pure Perfect Treasury.
Regarding "the treasury of adornments that illuminates all worlds":
because the internal, self-luminous, perfectly pure great wisdom radiates its extraordinary light, it is said to "illuminate all worlds."
It is called "ornamentation" because it is skillful and extraordinary;
it is called "ornamentation" because virtue arises from it;
therefore, it is named a "treasury."
One who practices the causal conduct of the essential nature is called a bodhisattva.
As for the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra,
he is a bodhisattva at the final stage of the mind of liberation-conduct.
Because he is the foremost among those addressed by this teaching who have been requested to set forth [the doctrine], his name alone is specifically cited.
Such a bodhisattva— this concludes the third major section, which next clarifies the number of such virtuous beings.
"Immeasurable" means that their status reaches the ultimate limit of existence.
"Boundless" means that their practice pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
"Asaṃkhyeya" (incalculable) means...
It transcends all limits.
That which is inconceivable clarifies that the essence is non-discriminative and free from discrimination.
"Inconceivable" (*asamkhyeya*) means that it is immeasurable, profound, heavy, and beyond reckoning.
"Immeasurable" (*aprameya*) means...
"Immeasurable" means boundless, vast, and incalculable.
"Without limits" refers to that which is asaṃkhyeya and unspeakable.
The explanation of the essence [of reality] is that it is neither conceptual differentiation nor a plurality of distinct entities.
That which cannot be expressed means it is free from conceptual differentiation, clarifying that it is not something diverse or manifold.
Upon investigation, this is not necessarily so.
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Incalculable Numbers" (*Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*):
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mind-King (*Cittarāja*) asked:
"What is meant by 'incalculable' (*asaṃkhyeya*), 'immeasurable,' 'without boundaries,' and 'without limits'?"
"It is incalculable, immeasurable, inconceivable, and ineffable.
The Buddha addressed Cittarāja Bodhisattva, saying:
"A hundred times a thousand, a hundred times a thousand, constitutes one *kuli*."
One *kuli-kuli* constitutes one *avikāra*.
One *avikāra-avikāra* is called one *nayuta*.
One *nayuta-nayuta* constitutes one *vibhava*.
Vipula-vipula is called one "making" (kṛti); kṛti-kṛti is called one "superior" (viśeṣa);
āgata-āgata is called one "superior."
One *jaya-jaya* is further called one *eka*;
one *eka* is further called one *apara*.
This continues until there are one hundred layers of *vedanā-vedanā* and so forth.
Thereafter, one reaches the *asaṃkhyeya*.
Following the *asaṃkhyeya*, there are further twenty-four layers of numerical calculation.
All of these are the methods for the practice within the *dharmadhātu* of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; indeed, even a single practice is vast and all-pervasive.
How can these characteristics be used to explain the absence of characteristics within the category of formations?
If one bases the meaning on the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), there is likewise no harm.
Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke in verse for the sake of King of Mind Bodhisattva:
Inexpressible and beyond description, throughout inexpressible eons,
one could not exhaustively describe what is inexpressible.
This clarifies the dharma-gate of the self-nature:
within unspeakably many atoms,
there are unspeakably many sentient beings.
All together they praise the virtues of Samantabhadra,
yet they cannot exhaust them; this clarifies the dharma-gate of the perfection of the virtues of practice and application.
Within each and every pore-path therein,
there are unspeakably many pure buddha-fields,
adorned with unspeakably many ornaments.
Adorning each of those various Buddha-fields,
this is the Dharma-door of the Collection of Methods for Integrating Principles and Clarifying the True Nature of Dependent Origination;
within each of those diverse colors, [it manifests].
Inexpressible sublime radiances are emitted;
from each and every one of those radiances,
inexpressible jewel lotuses emerge.
This is the Dharma-gate of Wisdom.
Within each of those precious lotus flowers,
there are unspeakably many precious petals.
Upon each and every petal of those jewel-flowers,
there are unspeakably many subtle colors,
which are the dharma-gates of the causal practices.
The Vajra-treasury is like Mount Sumeru;
pure, complete, and adorned.
Within each and every Sumeru...
There are unspeakably unspeakable gateways to the Dharma that clarify meritorious qualities;
within each and every one of those Brahma-voices, there are...
The ineffable wheel of purity can be described;
within each of those wheels of Dharma,
there are ineffable sūtras.
Elucidating the Dharma-gate of True Exegesis: These all clarify the characteristics of the differentiated functions and practices of the Dharma-realm.
Above, the World-Honored One answered Bodhisattva Mind-King with prose.

Regarding the number of hundreds of thousands and so forth, it is based on the distinctions in the categories and divisions of the collections of practices for cultivating remedies as they relate to their objects.
Below, the answer is given in verse:
because the application of the dharma-gates of the intrinsic nature of the *dharmadhātu* is vast and expansive, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*.
There are [levels] such as "unspeakable-unspeakable" and so forth;
how could these be awaited through mere names?
If one relies upon the three teachings:
Regarding these "numbers" of the Bodhisattvas:
if one relies on the teachings of transformation (hua-jiao), they are merely the phenomena themselves without any further distinction;
if one relies on the teachings of practice (xing-jiao), they are all the dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva's own essential nature.
Regarding "various Buddha-lands":
they are called "various" because the three kinds of worlds come forth from them.
Regarding "assembled": it is called "assembled" because the practices of Bodhisattvas gather together and manifest the characteristics of perfected virtues.
There are two meanings for Vajragarbha Bodhisattva being the leader (*agratas*).
First, he is the leader because his rank is ultimate, his practice is perfected, and his virtues surpass the great assembly.
Second, he is called the leader because the essence of all bodhisattvas' practices and virtues is truly real.
Furthermore, regarding the "foremost":
because the origin and development of the fundamental purpose of this school depend upon this person, he is established as the one who expounds the Dharma;
and because his manifest transformation and benefit for the times are most prominent at the beginning, he is placed at the outset.
It is said that Bodhisattva Vajragarbha was the leader.
